title: Prefetch recovery & warm-start heuristics - Monolith Analytics deep dive
summary: Monolith seeing intermittent p95/p99 tail spikes caused by KV paging and prefix reuse during long multi-turn conversations. Discussed warm-start (prefetch) tuning, fingerprint length, eviction strategies (LFU decay vs LRU), spill thresholds, and an on-prem pilot to eliminate remote spill. Agreed to run controlled bench and share redacted logs and a short SE playbook.
action_items: Grace - send p95/p99 token-level traces + sample eviction logs (redacted) by 2026-03-25
Monolith - export 1k representative sessions (anonymized) and mark incident traces by 2026-03-27
Diego - prepare SE config variants (prefetch=256/512, LFU_decay settings, fingerprint_len options) and bench plan by 2026-03-30
Samira - provision read-only Redwood Console view for Monolith and share access by 2026-03-26
next_steps: Run 3 bench variants in staging: baseline, larger prefetch + LFU, and conservative eviction + larger NVMe
Test private node pilot with increased local NVMe to observe tail removal
Share SOC2 and private-deploy security appendix and KMS integration docs
Follow-up call to review bench results and pick pilot config (tentative 2026-03-29)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62m
Attendees: Grace Li (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Samira N'Golo (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (CTO, Monolith), Priya Shah (Platform Eng), Rafael Mendes (SRE), Nora Bell (ML Eng)

Auto-summary (automated): Monolith reports intermittent long-tail latency and NVMe spills during multi-turn sessions that exceed ~8k tokens. Root cause candidates: prefix reuse causing cache churn, insufficient kv reserve, and remote spill latency. Agenda: warm-start/prefetch heuristics, eviction policy, spill tiering, fingerprinting, bench plan and compliance needs.

[00:00] Grace: hey all, thanks for joining, i'm Grace from Redwood. want to focus on the warm-start and prefetch side and get actionable knobs to reduce your tails. can you describe the worst-case pattern, Ethan?
[00:15] Ethan: yep, thanks. roughly we saw p95 move from 100-150ms to 700-1200ms intermittently. it correlated with heavy nvme writes on the inference nodes. sessions are multi-turn and sometimes users paste long docs so the session grows to 6-12k tokens.
[00:32] Diego: thanks, that pattern screams kv paging and on-demand reads. two common amplifiers: (1) prefix reuse where initial tokens are identical across many sessions, leading to fingerprint aliasing; (2) insufficient warmup prefetch that forces the runtime to pull kv blocks synchronously.
[00:47] Priya: quick Q - we are on Dedicated today with local nvme but no reserved burst, right?
[00:52] Nora: correct, 4 x A100, local NVMe, private control plane enabled. no extra burst reserve configured.
[00:59] Samira: ok, so a mix of storage pressure and reuse patterns. i'll sketch runtime behavior: we maintain a prefix index (fingerprints) and a kv block store; when a request arrives the runtime tries to hydrate kv for the next token slots. prefetch is async but if miss rate is high you get blocking i/o.
[01:18] Rafael: we saw small writes accumulating then a shift to large object-store writes and that's when latency exploded.
[01:24] Diego: that aligns - remote spill (S3-like) adds 150-600ms depending on region/latency. to avoid remote spill we have options: raise local nvme threshold, tune spill thresholds to spill earlier but in larger chunks, or increase kv memory reserve via quantization or model variant changes.
[01:42] Ethan: would increasing prefetch hurt memory?
[01:45] Diego: yes it trades memory/egress for lower on-demand i/o. default prefetch is 128 token slots; we can test 256 and 512. 256 often reduces p95 significantly in long-context repros but uses ~10-20% more kv memory bandwidth.
[02:02] Priya: prefix fingerprinting - how deep is it? we suspect collisions in first ~200 tokens across templates.
[02:08] Samira: default fingerprint seeds 64 bytes; increasing to 128 bytes reduces aliasing for template-heavy workloads but increases index RAM slightly. it's almost always worth it if templates share leading tokens.
[02:22] Rafael: what about LFU vs LRU? we want stable templates to stay cached, but also adapt to new ones.
[02:28] Diego: LFU with a decay (approx counts) = good compromise: retains steady templates while decaying obsolete ones. LRU reacts faster but will evict stable prefixes if thrashed. approximate counting sketches keep overhead low.
[02:43] Ethan: any short-term quick wins? we need something before the pilot.
[02:46] Grace: quick triage: (1) temporarily increase prefetch to 256 for heavy routes; (2) bump fingerprint_len to 128; (3) enable LFU_decay with a short decay (e.g., 60s) for your tenant; (4) increase NVMe stripe size so small writes coalesce. that suite usually reduces on-demand spikes within hours.
[03:10] Priya: tradeoffs: higher prefetch raises memory and egress; LFU can keep some stale entries if decay is too long; larger stripe size can defer writes but increase peak write latencies if NVMe is constrained. so monitor nvme_iowait and kv_miss_rate.
[03:28] Nora: how to reproduce quickly? we can supply a trace. what's most useful in the trace?
[03:33] Diego: session id (hashed), prefix fingerprint, token access sequence or token length histogram, and timestamps. we run a deterministic prefetch simulator that replays token accesses and shows miss patterns and simulated i/o.
[03:45] Rafael: ok we'll extract a 1k-session sample and mark incidents.
[03:50] Grace: great. about spill tiering - you mentioned object-store writes, is runtime doing remote spill immediately when NVMe crosses threshold?
[03:58] Samira: by default runtime spills to a warm-tier if NVMe crossing persists, but we can change policy to start early but in larger batches or to route to local warm-disk instead of remote object store when available. in on-prem you can often eliminate remote writes entirely by allocating enough local storage.
[04:17] Ethan: for compliance, we prefer on-prem but want minimal infra change. is private node with bigger NVMe a realistic pilot?
[04:23] Grace: yes, pilot with a private node + larger NVMe to observe whether tails vanish is a standard approach. we'll bench three variants and compare.
[04:31] Priya: question: quantization - if we run a quantized model variant will that free kv reserve? how tight is that coupling?
[04:37] Diego: quantization mainly reduces model memory footprint which can indirectly increase available kv capacity on the GPU. it doesn't reduce kv bytes directly, but freeing model RAM allows more kv blocks to stay in memory. aggressive quant can slightly slow per-token compute but often yields net p95 improvements for heavy-context loads.
[04:55] Rafael: thundering herd - we saw spikes when many sessions start the same template concurrently. any guardrails?
[05:00] Samira: options: tenant-scoped pre-warm queue to stagger warmups, server-side seeding of known hot prefixes during deploys, or allow client to send a low-cost warmup ping (a cheap request that triggers prefetch without full compute). Redwood router supports adaptive pacing to spread prefetch across nodes.
[05:18] Ethan: can we cap per-tenant prefetch concurrency?
[05:21] Diego: yes, per-tenant prefetch concurrency caps exist. that prevents a single tenant from saturating NVMe. we often pair that with a soft quota so you can burst briefly but don't thrash.
[05:33] Priya: telemetry - what dashboards/metrics should we watch?
[05:36] Grace: key signals: kv_miss_rate, spill_events (count + avg size), nvme_iowait, p95/p99 token latency, batch size distribution, prefix heatmap (hotness over time). we'll open a read-only Redwood Console view for you. Samira will provision it.
[05:53] Rafael: on logs - redact content, but keep session hashes and fingerprint ids; that's fine.
[05:57] Samira: we'll share a log bundle with request ids, shard ids, fingerprint ids, reason codes for eviction and timestamps. all request content will be redacted by default.
[06:06] Nora: fallback behavior - can runtime automatically move to a smaller model under sustained overload?
[06:10] Diego: yes we support policy-driven fallback to quantized or smaller model variants, can be triggered by sustained kv_miss_rate or high spill->remote rates. but you have to balance quality degradation. we recommend canarying with eval prompts.
[06:24] Ethan: rough expectations - if remote spill is the largest tail, how much improvement when removed?
[06:28] Grace: in our experience removing remote spill can cut p95 tails by 40-70% depending on workload shape; p99 becomes more variable but often halves when remote writes are eliminated.
[06:42] Priya: guardrails for unbounded kv growth - set session max-residency, sliding-window TTL for older context segments, and periodic checkpointing to compact context into snapshots then free detailed kv blocks. checkpoint frequency is a balance (e.g., every 1k tokens or every 5 minutes for high-churn sessions).
[06:59] Rafael: checkpointing I/O - will it add write pressure?
[07:02] Samira: yes but we do incremental checkpoints and prioritize background low-IO windows; still something to monitor.
[07:10] Grace: ok recap and timing: Monolith will provide dataset + incident slices; Redwood will run three bench variants and share results, SE playbook, and security appendix. target follow-up Tuesday 2026-03-29 10:00 UTC for bench review.
[07:28] Ethan: sounds good. one more ask: can you list the exact config knobs in the playbook? our infra team wants concrete values.
[07:33] Diego: yes, we'll include example knobs: prefetch_slots=256, fingerprint_len=128, eviction_policy=LFU_decay=60s, nvme_spill_threshold=70%, prefetch_concurrency_cap=8, checkpoint_every_tokens=1000. we'll also include a conservative variant.
[07:52] Priya: and we will include the telemetry queries to detect regressions.
[07:56] Rafael: thanks.
[08:00] Grace: any final questions?
[08:03] Nora: none here. thanks everyone.
[08:06] Grace: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts. meeting adjourned.

Transcript notes: occasional speaker merge and filler words ('uh', 'you know'), some technical terms transcribed as 'K-V' or 'key ve'.

Attachments referenced: bench-plan-template.csv (chat link), security-appendix-private-deploy.pdf (to be shared), sample-telemetry-query.gql (to be shared).
notes: Agreed pilot: private node with larger NVMe + prefetch=256 + LFU_decay; Redwood to run bench variants and share redacted logs and playbook.
